comments.comment: Summary of this video at 7:10. "You would never borrow on a paid for home to invest, and so you wouldn't keep a mortgage."

RE: 3:30 - Sorry, but the advice to pay off your mortgage when your mortgage rate is lower than the risk-free rate makes absolutely no sense at all.  If your mortgage is 3.25% AND you can take a tax write-off on the interest and you can instead take the money and buy risk-free US treasuries which are state tax-exempt...why would you throw that away?  I regret not borrowing more money on my mortgage back in 2021 and instead putting it into an index fund.  Only makes sense to pay off the mortgage if you are paying a high interest rate.  Also, not sure why he recommends fee-hungry mutual funds over low-cost index funds.

@4:20 This is a terrible evaluation of the numbers. Are millionaires millionaires because they have a paid off house or are millionaires able to pay off their house because they are millionaires. Paying down a mortgage doesn't make you a millionaire any faster than putting it into investments. In fact its slower.

David Suen David Suen David Suen I mean, paying off your house is never a bad thing but this isn’t advice that I would follow. There are certainly more efficient ways to leverage that money. Now that said, there is defiantly something to be said about paying off your house from an emotional stability standpoint like Dave mentioned at 6:05. Also, if you’re choosing between paying off your house or just wasting the money, paying off the house is defiantly better. But, that said, I think that at my young age l would ignore this advice and choose the option that allows me to leverage my money the most. I think Dave is incorrect in assuming that just because a lot of people do a certain thing that it is the best option mathematically because assuming a fixed 30 year morgagage, it’s usually mathematically better to leverage your money else where.

5:38 "So the data points tell us that the millionaires are paying off their house. Now why would they do that, because of risk. Because 100% of foreclosures happen on houses with a mortgage".  Except they don't. This is both anecdotally and factually incorrect. You can find lots of examples of "celebrities" who lose the houses they own outright to foreclosure because they can't afford to pay their property taxes (or the resulting tax lien) from previous years after their 15 minutes of fame is up. There are also many, MANY millionaires and billionaires, and especially money managers, who have mortgages, because it often doesn't make sense to have so much of your net worth (and liquidity) tied up in one asset, especially one that has appreciated so poorly over time, and when interest rates are so cheap.

I will give a scenario.  Then you decide.  In 2 years my house will be paid off if everything goes as planned.  At that point I can take SS and have a fully paid for home and not worry about foreclosure.  Yes I can keep working IF I WANT TO.  If I do  not pay off my house, and invest instead, I MIGHT have a good amount of cash invested, but I MUST keep working because I still have that huge mortgage.  See the difference?? Go to 3:36 for his answer.

5:45  Risk? Strange. The only risk I see is throwing all your money(besides your emergency fund) into your house when you could make a higher return just by keeping the mortgage.  Sounds like this dude has too much house too.

0:45 "And how much is the non-retirement nest egg?" That's an oxymoron. The only reason one has a nest egg is for retirement plus legacy (leaving to heirs), and by definition the latter is anything left over after the former. Dave may be thinking in terms of whether the money is in a fund that the government designates as having a tax benefit for retirement, but that has absolutely and precisely nothing to do with whether it is ACTUALLY "retirement" or "non-retirement".
At 5:40 100% of mortgage foreclosures happen to homes that have a mortgage. And this is why one would pay off their house. But why not move baby step 6 to baby step 1 or 2?
At around 2:39, he says to put 5% into Roth.  I thought if you earned $140,000 like this guy is, you can't put any money into Roth?

If the home is worth nothing after the fact of the mortgage it’s largely irrelevant to the decision to pay it off early since you still owe the bank the original sum. You’re saying he’s in imaginary negative equity or potential negative equity. Which is only useful information with either precognition or as 20:20 hindsight useless advice from a parallel universe where this has taken place
